essays.question: Some people believe that protecting the environment should be a top priority for governments. Others think that economic growth is more important. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether protecting the environment should be a top priority for governments or whether economic growth matters more. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, those who put economic growth first argue that strict environmental measures can raise costs for businesses and slow short-term growth. Factories must install cleaner equipment, and firms may respond by raising prices or cutting jobs. This matters most in poorer countries, where growth is needed to lift people out of poverty and to pay for hospitals and schools. A developing country that bans cheap coal before it has an alternative, for example, may leave millions of households without affordable electricity, and the resulting hardship can turn public opinion against environmental policy.

On the other hand, supporters of environmental protection point out that ignoring the environment is expensive in the long run. Floods, droughts and polluted air damage crops, homes and health, and the cost of cleaning up afterwards is usually far higher than the cost of preventing the damage. Environmental policy can also create growth, since renewable energy, insulation and recycling employ workers and encourage new technology. A city that invests in clean transport, for instance, reduces hospital costs from air pollution while creating jobs in construction and maintenance.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that environmental protection should take priority in the long term, because growth built on damage cannot last, although governments should introduce measures gradually so that businesses and poorer households have time to adapt.

grade.summary: Bài viết của bạn có chất lượng tốt, đạt tiêu chuẩn cấu trúc và ngữ pháp của IELTS Writing Task 2. Việc lập luận mạch lạc và có ví dụ minh họa giúp bài viết thuyết phục, chỉ cần chú ý tinh chỉnh thêm một vài lỗi nhỏ về diễn đạt.

Một số từ vựng mang tính phổ biến cao, chưa có nhiều từ vựng cấp độ C1/C2 thực sự nổi bật.

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời tốt yêu cầu của đề bài khi thảo luận cả hai quan điểm và đưa ra ý kiến cá nhân rõ ràng. Các luận điểm được phát triển logic với ví dụ thực tế cụ thể, mặc dù phần quan điểm cá nhân ở kết bài có thể được bàn luận sâu hơn một chút ở thân bài.

essays.question: Some people prefer environmentally friendly products while others prefer cheaper alternatives. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether people should buy environmentally friendly products or choose cheaper alternatives. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of green products argue that environmentally friendly products reduce harm and often save money over time. They use less energy, create less waste and are often more durable, and growing demand encourages companies to improve their methods. An efficient light bulb, for example, may cost more at first but lasts much longer and uses far less electricity. Buyers who choose such goods also send a clear signal to manufacturers that the market wants cleaner production. If enough people do this, prices tend to fall and green options become normal.

On the other hand, others point out that many households simply cannot afford to pay extra for green products. When budgets are tight, families have to choose the cheapest option, and for people on low incomes the price on the label matters more than long-term benefits. Some products labelled green make claims that are exaggerated or hard to check, so shoppers may pay more without any real gain for the environment. Cheap alternatives therefore remain popular unless prices fall or rules improve. A parent who is buying clothes and food for a family of five, for instance, cannot always choose the more expensive version.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that people should choose green products where they can afford them, while governments should make them cheaper through taxes and clear labelling so that the choice becomes easier for everyone.

grade.summary: Bài viết đạt chất lượng tốt, cấu trúc mạch lạc, ngữ pháp vững vàng và từ vựng phong phú bám sát chủ đề. Để đạt điểm cao hơn, người viết cần tinh chỉnh một số collocation và đào sâu hơn vào các lập luận kinh tế.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for pollution, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether individuals should take responsibility for pollution or whether society and governments should act. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, those who stress personal responsibility argue that everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Millions of households decide how much they drive, how much rubbish they produce and which products they buy, and these habits determine how much pollution is created. Consumers who choose cleaner products also push companies to change, since firms follow demand. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A commuter who swaps a daily car journey for a bicycle, for example, removes a small but real source of exhaust fumes, and many people doing the same would make a noticeable difference to the air in a city.

On the other hand, supporters of government action point out that individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. A person cannot choose a clean power station or a factory that filters its emissions, and the biggest sources of pollution are often industries rather than households. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as emission limits and fines, which create a level playing field so that responsible firms are not undercut by careless ones. They can also build the public transport and waste systems that make green choices practical. A resident of a town with no reliable buses, for instance, has little choice but to drive.

In conclusion, both sides have a point. Personally, I believe that governments should take the lead because they control the rules and the infrastructure, while individuals play a complementary role by supporting and following them.

essays.question: In your opinion, should countries invest more in renewable energy? Explain why.

versions.text:
Rising fuel prices and worries about pollution have made energy a central political issue. I firmly believe that countries should invest more in renewable energy, since it reduces pollution and carbon emissions and also strengthens energy security.

To begin with, renewable energy is cleaner than coal, oil and gas. Solar panels and wind turbines produce electricity without burning fuel, so they release almost no greenhouse gases and none of the smoke that harms people's lungs in crowded cities. The sun and wind will not run out, whereas fossil fuels are limited and their extraction damages land and water. A city that replaces a coal power station with wind and solar farms, for example, can breathe cleaner air within a few years, and hospitals may treat fewer patients with breathing problems.

Furthermore, investing in renewables makes a country less dependent on imported fuel. Nations that buy oil and gas from abroad are exposed to sudden price rises and political disputes, while home-grown wind and solar power gives them a more stable and secure supply. Spending on renewable technology also creates employment in manufacturing, installation and maintenance, and the cost of solar and wind equipment has fallen as the technology has improved. Admittedly, the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, so countries need batteries and flexible grids, but this cost is modest compared with the benefits. Over time, cheaper clean power can also help ordinary households and businesses to cut their energy bills.

In conclusion, I believe that countries should invest more in renewable energy, because it is cleaner, more secure and increasingly affordable.

grade.summary: Bài viết của bạn rất mạch lạc, bố cục rõ ràng và lập luận sắc bén về chủ đề năng lượng tái tạo. Với độ dài 268 từ, bài viết đã đáp ứng tốt yêu cầu tối thiểu và đạt mức điểm khá cao về mọi tiêu chí.
weaknesses: Một số từ vựng còn mang tính phổ biến, thiếu các cụm từ ăn ý (collocations) nâng cao
Phần kết luận lặp lại ý của mở bài hơi nhiều mà chưa mở rộng thêm góc nhìn sâu sắc hơn

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết trả lời trực tiếp câu hỏi của đề bài, có lập trường rõ ràng ngay từ phần mở bài và phát triển các ý chính rất tốt. Các luận điểm về môi trường và an ninh năng lượng được hỗ trợ bằng các ví dụ và lý lẽ thuyết phục.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc với cấu trúc 4 đoạn rõ ràng. Các từ nối và phương tiện liên kết được sử dụng hiệu quả để dẫn dắt người đọc qua các ý tưởng.

feedback.grammar: Đa dạng các cấu trúc câu phức và câu ghép với độ chính xác cao. Ngữ pháp và các thì được kiểm soát tốt xuyên suốt bài viết.

Câu chủ đề đặt thẳng ý (renewable energy is cleaner…), cơ chế (không đốt nhiên liệu), kết quả (không khí sạch hơn), ví dụ (thành phố thay nhà máy than bằng điện gió).

crossCheck.summary: Bài viết mạnh, trả lời đúng trọng tâm đề và duy trì lập trường xuyên suốt. Từ vựng và ngữ pháp ở mức tốt, bố cục chặt chẽ. Để nâng band, thí sinh nên làm cho ví dụ cụ thể hơn và tinh chỉnh một số collocation.

essays.question: How can governments encourage recycling? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Recycling saves raw materials and keeps rubbish out of landfill, yet in many places a large share of recyclable material is still thrown away. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on making recycling easy and on giving people a reason to take part.

To begin with, governments should make recycling convenient. Households are more likely to sort their rubbish if collection is regular, bins are clearly marked and the rules are simple. Colour-coded containers, weekly kerbside collection and public recycling points in busy areas remove the effort from the process. Only governments can build the sorting plants and collection networks that make recycling practical. A resident with no collection point nearby, for example, has little chance of recycling even when they want to. Clear labels on packaging, which show what can be recycled, would also reduce confusion.

In addition, authorities should give people good reasons to take part. Deposit schemes, in which customers receive a small refund for returning bottles and cans, raise return rates sharply, and lower charges for households that produce less general waste reward careful sorting. Education campaigns in schools and on local media explain why recycling matters and how to do it correctly. Equally important, governments can require manufacturers to use recycled material, which creates a market for what households collect. A council that publishes how much material each neighbourhood recycles, for instance, can encourage friendly competition and steady improvement. These steps cost little compared with the expense of extracting new raw materials.

In conclusion, making recycling convenient and rewarding, through better services, deposits, education and demand for recycled materials, offers the most realistic way of increasing participation.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for conserving water, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Water shortages are becoming more common in many regions, and people disagree about who should be responsible for conserving water. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, some argue that individuals should save water because everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Households use water for showers, washing machines and gardens, and simple habits such as turning off taps, fixing leaks and collecting rainwater can reduce consumption considerably. Consumers who buy water-efficient appliances also push manufacturers to improve their designs. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A family that repairs a dripping tap and takes shorter showers, for example, may save thousands of litres a year, and if a whole neighbourhood follows, the effect on local supplies becomes significant.

On the other hand, others believe that governments must act because individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. Much of a city's water is lost through ageing pipes that only the utility can replace, and farming and industry use far more than households. Authorities can set rules that apply to everyone, such as limits during droughts, higher prices for heavy users and fines for waste, and only they can build reservoirs, treatment plants and efficient irrigation. A city that loses a third of its water through old pipes, for instance, wastes more than its residents could ever save.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that the most effective approach combines official leadership with personal action, as governments should repair the system while citizens supply the daily decisions that make policies work.

essays.question: How far do you think renewable energy will change in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Solar panels and wind turbines have moved from the margins to the centre of energy planning in many countries. I believe that renewable energy will change considerably over the next twenty years, becoming cheaper, more reliable and far more widely used, although fossil fuels will not disappear completely.

First and foremost, technology and costs are moving in a favourable direction. The cost of solar and wind equipment has fallen as the technology has improved and factories have grown larger, and further progress is likely to make clean power competitive with coal and gas almost everywhere. As a result, utilities and households will choose renewables on price alone, without needing generous subsidies. A homeowner who installs solar panels, for example, may soon recover the cost through lower electricity bills within a few years.

In addition, storage and smarter grids will help to solve the problem that the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow. Better batteries can store surplus energy for use at night or in calm weather, and flexible grids can balance supply and demand across large areas. These improvements will make renewable power dependable enough to supply a large share of electricity. However, change will have limits. Heavy industry, aviation and shipping are hard to run on electricity, and many developing countries still rely on cheap coal. Old power stations also last for decades, so the shift will be gradual rather than sudden.

In conclusion, renewable energy is likely to change the way the world produces power to a large extent, thanks to falling costs and better storage, although a full transition will take longer than twenty years.

grade.summary: Bài viết có chất lượng khá tốt, bố cục chặt chẽ và lập luận rõ ràng về sự phát triển của năng lượng tái tạo trong 20 năm tới. Từ vựng và ngữ pháp được sử dụng ở mức độ ổn định, đáp ứng tốt yêu cầu của đề bài.

essays.question: To what extent should environmental protection influence government policy? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Governments must balance many aims, from jobs to security, and some people argue that environmental protection should shape policy in every area. I largely agree, since ignoring the environment is expensive in the long run and many problems cannot be solved by markets alone, although it should not override all other goals.

To begin with, the damage caused by neglect is costly. Floods, droughts and polluted air harm crops, homes and health, and the cost of cleaning up afterwards is usually far higher than the cost of preventing the damage. A government that allows a river to become heavily polluted, for example, must later pay for water treatment and for the illnesses that follow, which wastes money that could have funded schools or hospitals. Taking the environment into account when planning policy therefore protects public finances as well as nature.

Furthermore, only governments can set rules that apply to everyone. Individual companies and households have little reason to cut pollution if their competitors do not, so taxes, limits and fines are needed to create a level playing field. Policy can also create growth and employment, since renewable energy, insulation and recycling employ workers and encourage new technology. However, environmental concerns cannot be the only factor. Poorer countries need affordable energy and jobs, and unrealistic rules may cause hardship or political opposition. Policies should therefore be introduced gradually and supported by help for the communities that are affected most.

In conclusion, environmental protection should influence government policy to a large extent, because it saves money in the long term and requires collective rules, provided that its costs are shared fairly.

essays.question: Many people say that single-use plastics should be banned. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Plastic cups, bags and straws are used for a few minutes and then thrown away, and many people say that single-use plastics should be banned. I agree with this view, since these items cause lasting damage to nature and there are practical alternatives for almost all of them.

To begin with, plastic persists in the environment for centuries. Single-use items rarely decompose; instead they break into tiny pieces called microplastics, which are found in rivers, soil and even the food that people eat. Marine animals such as turtles and seabirds swallow plastic or become trapped in it, and cleaning oceans afterwards is extremely difficult and costly. Because these products are used only once, the scale of the problem grows every year. A beach covered with bottles and bags, for example, harms wildlife and also discourages tourists, which damages the local economy.

Furthermore, bans work when alternatives exist, and for most single-use plastics they do. Paper bags, cloth shopping bags, metal straws and reusable bottles perform the same function and can be used many times. When shops in several countries introduced a small charge for plastic bags, for instance, their use fell sharply, which shows that people adapt quickly once the habit is changed. Admittedly, a ban may raise costs for some businesses and could be difficult to enforce among small sellers, but this problem can be eased by giving firms time to switch and by supporting cheaper substitutes. Over time, the new habits become normal and the benefits for rivers, beaches and wildlife become clear.

In conclusion, I agree that single-use plastics should be banned, because they cause lasting harm and sensible alternatives are available, provided that the ban is introduced gradually.

essays.question: Some argue that public transport is the main way to reduce pollution. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Traffic jams and exhaust fumes make air pollution a daily problem in many cities, and some people argue that public transport is the main way to reduce it. I partly agree, since public transport can cut pollution significantly, but it is one of several measures rather than the only answer.

To begin with, public transport carries many people with far less pollution per passenger. A full bus or train replaces dozens of cars, which reduces exhaust fumes, congestion and the space needed for roads. Cities with frequent, reliable and affordable services often see fewer private cars on the road, and the air in busy streets becomes cleaner and quieter. A commuter who switches from a car to a tram, for example, cuts their share of emissions every day. Public transport also saves time and money, so people are more likely to continue using it.

However, public transport is not the main way to reduce pollution on its own. Much pollution comes from factories, power stations and heating, which buses and trains do not affect. Even within transport, other measures matter: electric vehicles remove tailpipe emissions, cycling and walking produce none, and better urban planning reduces the distances that people need to travel. Public transport also works only if it is convenient, and in low-density areas, services can be infrequent and expensive to run. A town where buses run once an hour, for instance, cannot persuade many drivers to leave their cars at home.

In conclusion, public transport is an important way to reduce pollution, but it works best alongside cleaner industry, electric vehicles and good city planning, so I agree only partly with the statement.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on green technology? Use examples.

versions.text:
Green technology, such as electric vehicles, solar panels and energy-saving machines, is attracting a growing amount of investment. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on it: a cleaner environment with lower costs, and new industries and exports.

First and foremost, green technology improves the environment while saving money. Efficient buildings, appliances and factories use less energy, so they reduce both pollution and bills, and clean transport cuts the exhaust fumes that damage health in crowded cities. As a result, the country spends less on imported fuel and on treating illnesses caused by dirty air. A city that replaces diesel buses with electric ones, for example, enjoys quieter streets and cleaner air, and its transport company spends less on fuel in the long run.

In addition, green technology creates new industries and jobs. Companies that design batteries, smart meters or wind turbines employ engineers, factory workers and installers, and a country that develops expertise early can sell its products abroad. A country that becomes known for efficient batteries, for instance, can sell them to many others. Because other countries are also trying to reduce emissions, demand for these products is likely to keep growing. Although the initial investment is high, the long-term returns in jobs, savings and exports are considerable, and they are likely to rise as the technology becomes cheaper and more widespread.

To sum up, green technology brings clear benefits to a country, above all a cleaner environment with lower costs and a stronger, more competitive economy. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: How can governments reduce plastic waste? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Plastic waste is polluting oceans, rivers and land in almost every country. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on reducing the production of plastic items and on improving recycling and clean-up.

To begin with, governments can reduce the amount of plastic that enters the market. Banning or taxing single-use items such as bags, cups and straws encourages people to switch to reusable alternatives, and requiring manufacturers to use less packaging cuts waste at its source. A small charge for plastic bags, for example, has reduced their use sharply in several countries. Governments can also require producers to pay for the collection and recycling of the packaging they sell, which gives companies a reason to design products that are easier to recycle and to avoid unnecessary wrapping altogether.

In addition, authorities should improve collection and recycling systems. Deposit schemes, in which customers receive a small refund for returning bottles, raise return rates and keep bottles out of the environment. Investment in sorting plants and regular collection makes recycling practical for households, and public education campaigns explain which items can be recycled. Equally important, clean-up programmes and stricter penalties for dumping protect rivers and beaches. A town that offers a refund for every returned bottle, for instance, often finds that litter along its streets falls and that the material is reused instead of wasted. These measures are not expensive compared with the long-term cost of polluted seas and damaged wildlife.

In conclusion, reducing plastic production through bans, charges and producer responsibility, and improving recycling through deposits and better infrastructure, offer the most realistic way of cutting plastic waste.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for reducing their carbon footprint, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Climate change has made many people ask who should be responsible for reducing carbon emissions: individuals or society as a whole. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Millions of households decide how they travel, how they heat their homes and what they eat, and flying less, eating less meat and using energy-saving appliances can cut a family's carbon footprint significantly. Consumers who choose low-carbon products also push companies to change, since firms follow demand. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A commuter who swaps a daily car journey for a bicycle, for example, avoids a noticeable amount of exhaust gas each year, and the savings multiply when a whole workplace joins in.

On the other hand, advocates of collective action point out that individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. Most emissions come from power stations, factories and transport systems that people cannot redesign themselves, and a customer cannot choose clean electricity if the grid still burns coal. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as carbon taxes and efficiency standards, and only they can build the public transport and renewable power networks that make green choices practical. A resident of a town with no reliable buses or trains, for instance, has little choice but to drive.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that governments should take the lead, since they control the rules and the infrastructure, while individuals make policies work through their daily decisions.

essays.question: To what extent should corporations be responsible for environmental damage? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Large companies produce much of the world's pollution and waste, and I largely agree that they should be held responsible for the damage they cause, although governments and consumers also have a part to play.

To begin with, polluters should pay for the damage they cause. When a factory releases waste into a river and the cost of the clean-up falls on taxpayers, the company profits while the public pays, which is unfair. Fines, clean-up charges and taxes make firms include environmental costs in their prices, and this gives them a reason to adopt cleaner methods. Corporations that profit from an activity should bear the cost of its damage, and those with large budgets can usually afford to do so. A chemical company that knows it will pay for any spill, for example, will invest more in safety, because prevention becomes cheaper than compensation.

Furthermore, companies have the knowledge and resources to find solutions. They control their own production, choose their materials and design their packaging, so changes at this level affect millions of products at once, which individual shoppers cannot achieve. However, corporations are not solely to blame. Consumers demand cheap goods, and governments must set clear rules so that responsible firms are not undercut by careless ones. Responsibility should therefore be shared, with businesses carrying the largest part, and with independent inspection to make sure that promises are kept.

In conclusion, corporations should be responsible for environmental damage to a large extent, because they cause it and profit from it, provided that governments enforce fair rules.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear energy.

versions.text:
Nuclear power supplies a significant share of electricity in several countries, yet it remains controversial. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, nuclear plants produce large amounts of low-carbon electricity. A single plant can run day and night whatever the weather, so it provides steady power that wind and solar cannot always guarantee, and it releases almost no greenhouse gases while operating. Because a small amount of fuel produces a great deal of energy, countries can also reduce their dependence on imported coal and gas. A country with several reactors, for example, can keep its lights on during a calm, cloudy week without burning fossil fuels. Plants also last for sixty years or more, which gives a long period of stable production.

On the negative side, nuclear power carries serious risks and costs. Accidents are rare, but the consequences of a nuclear accident can be severe and long-lasting, as the disasters at Chernobyl and Fukushima showed. Radioactive waste must also be stored safely for thousands of years, which places a burden on future generations. In addition, plants are very expensive and often take over a decade to build, so they may be completed late and over budget. Safe operation requires strict regulation and highly trained staff, which poorer countries may find difficult to provide.

In conclusion, nuclear energy offers reliable low-carbon power, but its dangers, waste and cost are serious drawbacks. On balance, I believe that it should be one part of a mixed energy supply in countries with strong safety systems, rather than the main solution.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for protecting wildlife, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
The loss of habitats and species raises the question of who should be responsible for protecting wildlife: ordinary people, or governments and society. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, some argue that individuals have a duty to protect wildlife because everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. People decide whether to buy products made from endangered animals, whether to leave rubbish in natural areas and whether to support conservation charities. Gardeners who plant native flowers and leave small wild corners also give insects and birds a place to live. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A hiker who takes litter home and keeps to marked paths, for example, causes far less disturbance to nesting birds, and if thousands of visitors behave in the same way the damage to a reserve is greatly reduced.

On the other hand, others claim that governments must lead because individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. The greatest threats to wildlife, such as the clearing of forests, industrial pollution and large-scale illegal hunting, are far beyond the reach of personal action. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as protected reserves and heavy penalties for poaching, and only they can fund the rangers and monitoring that make these rules real. A national park without enough guards, for instance, soon becomes a hunting ground.

In conclusion, both sides are partly right. I believe that governments should take the lead, since they control the law and the funding, while individuals make protection work by following the rules and supporting it.

essays.question: How can governments improve urban green spaces? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Cities offer jobs and services, but many of them lack parks, trees and open space, which makes life hotter, noisier and less healthy. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on protecting and creating green space and on keeping it well maintained and accessible.

To begin with, governments can protect and expand green space inside cities. Planning rules can protect existing parks, require new developments to include gardens and playgrounds, and encourage green roofs and street trees where land is scarce. Unused sites, such as old car parks or empty plots, can be turned into small parks at low cost. A block of flats with a planted roof, for example, stays cooler in summer and offers residents a small garden. Over time, a network of connected green areas can help to cool the city, absorb pollution and shelter birds and insects.

In addition, authorities should make sure that green spaces are well maintained and accessible to everyone. Parks that are dirty or unsafe are rarely used, so councils need to budget for cleaning, lighting, repair and sensible security. Facilities such as paths, benches and play areas should be suitable for children, older people and people with disabilities, and parks should be located in poorer districts as well as wealthy ones. Equally important, involving residents in the design and care of their local park, through volunteer groups or consultations, encourages pride and reduces vandalism. These measures are inexpensive compared with the health and social benefits that they bring.

In conclusion, protecting and creating green spaces and then maintaining them for all residents offers the most realistic way of improving urban green areas.

essays.question: Many feel that food packaging is too wasteful. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Fruit sealed in plastic trays, snacks wrapped twice and online parcels filled with extra padding are familiar sights, and many people feel that food packaging is too wasteful. I largely agree, although some packaging does protect food.

To begin with, much food packaging is excessive. Products are often wrapped in several layers, such as a box, a plastic tray and a film, when one layer would be enough, and large boxes are used for small items. Much packaging exists for marketing rather than protection, and most of this material is thrown away within minutes. A large share cannot be recycled because it mixes different plastics. A cucumber wrapped in plastic, for example, already has its own natural skin, so the extra layer adds waste without adding protection. Over a year, such small choices add up to huge quantities of rubbish.

Furthermore, wasteful packaging creates avoidable pollution and costs. Producing and transporting packaging uses energy and raw materials, and litter from takeaway containers pollutes streets and waterways. Consumers pay for the packaging in the price, and councils pay to collect it. However, some packaging is necessary. It protects food from damage, keeps it hygienic and can extend its shelf life, which reduces food waste. Companies should therefore keep protective packaging but cut the unnecessary extras, and use materials that are easier to recycle or reuse. Refill stations and loose products, for instance, allow shoppers to buy only what they need in their own containers, which saves both money and materials.

In conclusion, I largely agree that food packaging is too wasteful, since much of it is unnecessary, although essential protection for food should be kept.

essays.question: How far do you think renewable energy will replace fossil fuels in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
With fossil fuels still supplying most of the world's energy, many people ask how far renewable sources can replace them in the next twenty years. I believe that they will replace fossil fuels only in part: renewables are likely to dominate electricity generation, but oil and gas will remain in heavy industry and transport.

To begin with, there are strong reasons for a rapid shift in electricity. Solar and wind power are already cheaper than coal in many places, they release almost no greenhouse gases, and governments are setting targets to cut emissions. As costs fall and batteries improve, power companies will keep building clean capacity instead of new coal stations. A country that closes its last coal plants and builds wind farms off its coast, for example, can supply a large share of its electricity from renewables within twenty years.

However, replacing fossil fuels completely is far more difficult. Steel, cement, aviation and shipping need very high temperatures or fuels that are dense and light, and electricity cannot yet do these jobs at a reasonable price. In addition, the sun does not always shine and the wind does not always blow, so grids need large amounts of storage and backup power. Many developing countries also depend on cheap coal and oil to grow their economies, and power stations and pipelines built today will operate for decades. These factors mean that change will be uneven across regions and sectors. A factory that makes steel, for instance, cannot switch to wind power in a few years.

In conclusion, renewable energy will replace fossil fuels to a considerable but incomplete extent over the next twenty years, mainly in electricity, while heavy industry and long-distance transport lag behind.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of genetically modified crops.

versions.text:
Genetically modified crops, whose genes have been altered in a laboratory to give them useful traits, are widely grown in some countries and banned in others. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, genetically modified crops can produce higher and more reliable yields. Plants can be changed to resist pests, tolerate drought or contain extra vitamins, so farmers lose less of their harvest and need fewer chemicals. More food is then grown on the same land, which helps a growing population. A farmer who plants a drought-resistant variety, for example, may still harvest a reasonable crop in a dry year, when ordinary seed would fail. Crops improved in this way can also reduce hunger and malnutrition in poorer regions.

On the negative side, however, the long-term effects of genetically modified crops are not fully known. Modified genes could spread to wild plants, and farmers who buy patented seed each year become dependent on a few large companies. Many consumers distrust modified food, and people in some countries worry about its safety even though the evidence so far is limited. Nevertheless, these concerns can be addressed. Careful testing, independent regulation and clear labels would allow consumers to make their own choices and would help to detect problems early.

In conclusion, genetically modified crops offer real benefits for food supply, but uncertainty about long-term effects and corporate control are valid concerns. On balance, I believe that they should be used cautiously, under strict testing and open information.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for recycling, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Recycling is widely encouraged, yet people disagree about whether it is mainly a personal duty or something that society and governments should organise. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Households decide whether to sort glass, paper and plastic or to throw everything into one bin, and careless sorting can spoil whole loads of recyclable material. Shoppers who choose products with less packaging also push companies to reduce waste. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A family that separates its rubbish carefully every week, for example, keeps a large amount of material out of landfill, and a street where everyone does the same can cut its waste dramatically.

On the other hand, advocates of collective action point out that individuals alone cannot recycle what the system cannot process. A household cannot build a sorting plant or create a market for recycled materials, and many people live in areas where collection is irregular or unavailable. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as deposit schemes and requirements for manufacturers to use recycled content, and only they can build the infrastructure that makes recycling practical. A resident with no collection point nearby, for instance, has little chance of recycling even when they want to.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that the most effective approach combines official leadership with personal action, since government provides the system and citizens supply the daily effort that makes it work.

essays.question: What are the causes of air pollution in industrial cities? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
Industrial cities offer jobs and growth, but their air is often thick with smoke and dust. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Factories, coal power stations and traffic are the main causes of air pollution in industrial cities. They release smoke, dust and gases such as sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, and the problem is worse when cities are crowded or surrounded by hills that trap polluted air. A city with many coal-burning factories in a valley, for example, may be covered in smog for weeks in winter. In addition, old vehicles and heavy lorries add fumes to the air at street level, and construction work and open burning of waste raise the amount of dust. Residents then suffer from breathing problems and heart disease, and the cost of health care rises.

To address this issue, strict emission limits and cleaner energy would reduce air pollution. Filters and emission limits cut what factories release, clean electricity from wind, solar and gas can replace coal, and better public transport and electric vehicles reduce traffic fumes. Governments should enforce these rules with inspections and meaningful fines, and help small firms to afford cleaner equipment. In addition, air quality monitoring and green belts help to track progress and absorb pollutants, and public warnings allow vulnerable people to protect themselves on bad days. Cities that have cleaned their air in this way have usually found that the improvement in health and productivity more than repays the cost.

In conclusion, air pollution in industrial cities stems mainly from factories, coal power and traffic, but strict limits, cleaner energy and monitoring offer a realistic way forward.

essays.question: Some people believe that climate change is mainly caused by human activity. Others think natural factors are more significant. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether climate change is mainly caused by human activity or whether natural factors are more significant. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, those who emphasise natural factors point out that the climate has always changed through natural causes. Volcanic eruptions, variations in the sun's energy and shifts in ocean currents produced warm periods and ice ages long before humans existed. Some people therefore argue that today's warming may be part of a natural cycle, and that human influence is exaggerated. This view also reminds us that climate science is complex, and that scientists continue to study natural variation in order to improve their predictions.

On the other hand, supporters of the human-activity explanation argue that scientific evidence links the recent rise in temperatures to human activity. Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests release gases that trap heat, and temperatures have risen alongside emissions since the industrial era began. Natural cycles, which operate over thousands of years, cannot explain such rapid warming. A greenhouse works in a similar way, which is why these gases are said to warm the planet. In addition, studies of past climates show that the present rate of change is unusually fast.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that human activity is the main cause, since the speed of the current warming cannot be explained by natural cycles, although natural factors still shape the climate.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on renewable resources? Use examples.

versions.text:
Many countries are shifting from coal, oil and gas towards solar, wind and water power. This essay will outline two principal benefits of focusing on renewable resources: a cleaner and healthier environment, and greater energy security and economic opportunity.

First and foremost, renewable energy improves the environment and public health. Solar panels and wind turbines produce electricity without burning fuel, so they release almost no greenhouse gases and none of the smoke that harms people's lungs in crowded cities. As a result, the air is cleaner, hospitals treat fewer patients with breathing problems, and the country contributes to the effort to slow climate change. Denmark, for example, generates a large share of its electricity from wind, which shows that a small country can reduce its reliance on fossil fuels. A city that replaces a coal power station with wind and solar farms may notice clearer skies within a few years.

In addition, renewable resources make a country more secure and more prosperous. Nations that buy oil and gas from abroad are exposed to sudden price rises and political disputes, whereas home-grown wind and solar power gives them a stable and secure supply. The sector also creates employment in manufacturing, installation and maintenance, and countries that develop expertise early can sell equipment and skills to others. Because the sun and wind will not run out, these benefits last for future generations. Although renewable power needs storage and flexible grids, these costs are falling as technology improves.

To sum up, focusing on renewable resources brings clear benefits to a country, above all a cleaner environment and a more secure economy. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Many people say that public gardens should be protected from development. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
As cities grow, public gardens are sometimes sold for housing or shops, and many people say that they should be protected from development. I agree with this view, since gardens give city residents health, shade and a place to meet that cannot easily be replaced.

To begin with, public gardens give city residents health, shade and a place to meet. They cool the air in summer, absorb dust and pollution, shelter birds and insects and offer free space to rest, exercise and play. For people who live in flats without a garden, these places are often the only contact with nature. A small garden in a crowded district, for example, may be used every day by older residents, parents with young children and office workers on their lunch break. Studies of many cities suggest that access to green space improves physical and mental health.

Furthermore, once a garden has been built over, it is almost impossible to replace. New trees need decades to mature, and the history and community life of the site are lost for good. Housing, by contrast, can usually be built on empty or abandoned sites, or on land that has already been developed, so protecting gardens does not mean stopping growth. Admittedly, cities need more homes and economic activity, and some gardens may be poorly used or badly kept. In such cases, authorities should improve them instead of selling them, and any development that does take place should be limited and balanced by new green space elsewhere.

In conclusion, I agree that public gardens should be protected from development, because they are valuable and irreplaceable, although well-planned building on other sites should continue.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on renewable transport? Use examples.

versions.text:
Cars, buses and lorries that run on petrol and diesel are a major source of pollution. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on renewable transport, such as electric vehicles, trains and bicycles: cleaner air and better health, and lower dependence on imported fuel.

First and foremost, renewable transport improves air quality and public health. Electric buses and cars produce no exhaust fumes on the road, and when their power comes from wind or solar they release far fewer greenhouse gases over their lifetime. As a result, residents of crowded cities breathe cleaner air, noise levels fall and fewer people suffer from breathing problems. A city that replaces diesel buses with electric ones, for example, enjoys quieter streets and cleaner air, and its centre becomes a more pleasant place to walk, shop and live.

In addition, renewable transport makes a country more secure and more economical. Nations that buy oil from abroad are exposed to sudden price rises and political disputes, whereas home-grown electricity gives them a more stable supply. Electric vehicles also cost less to run, because electricity is usually cheaper than fuel per kilometre and they need less maintenance. The country can create jobs in building charging points, public transport and cycle routes, and manufacturers that lead in electric vehicles can sell them abroad. Although charging networks and cleaner power grids require large investment, the long-term savings are considerable.

To sum up, renewable transport brings clear benefits to a country, above all cleaner air and a more secure, lower-cost transport system. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: To what extent should animal welfare laws be strengthened? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Animals are kept on farms, in zoos, in laboratories and in homes, and some people argue that the laws protecting them should be stronger. I largely agree, since animals can feel pain and fear, although laws must also take account of human needs.

To begin with, animals can feel pain and fear, so they deserve legal protection. Weak laws allow cruelty on farms, in circuses and in laboratories, whereas strong laws set minimum standards of care and penalties for those who break them. In some places, for example, hens may be kept in tiny cages for their entire lives, and a law that bans such cages forces producers to give animals room to move. Without legal limits, businesses that want to cut costs may be tempted to ignore suffering, and honest producers are undercut by careless ones.

Furthermore, clear rules reflect the values of a modern society. Most people agree that causing needless suffering is wrong, yet individuals cannot inspect farms or laboratories themselves, so only inspectors acting under strict laws can ensure that standards are kept. Better conditions can also lead to healthier animals and safer food. However, the laws must be realistic. Farmers who face higher costs may need time and financial support to adapt, and some research that depends on animals may save human lives, so such work should be allowed under strict supervision. Strong laws should therefore protect animals without ignoring the needs of people who depend on them.

In conclusion, animal welfare laws should be strengthened to a large extent, because animals can suffer and weak rules allow cruelty, provided that the changes are introduced fairly.

essays.question: How can governments reduce littering in public places? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Crisp packets, cigarette ends and drink containers left on streets and in parks spoil public spaces and harm wildlife. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on making it easy to dispose of rubbish properly and on discouraging people who drop it.

To begin with, governments should make proper disposal easy. People are more likely to use a bin if one is close by, so councils should place well-marked bins in busy streets, near bus stops and at park entrances, and empty them often so that they do not overflow. Separate containers for recycling and general rubbish, with clear symbols, help people to do the right thing quickly. A park with a bin every fifty metres, for example, will usually be cleaner than one with only a few. Clean surroundings also set an example, because people tend to drop rubbish where litter already exists, so regular cleaning is part of the solution.

In addition, authorities should discourage careless behaviour. Visible fines for dropping litter, supported by patrols or cameras in problem areas, make people think twice, and community service for repeat offenders can be an effective penalty. Equally important, public campaigns and school lessons can change attitudes by explaining the harm that litter causes to animals and neighbourhoods. Deposit schemes for bottles and cans also give containers a value, so that people return them instead of dropping them. A town that combines more bins, fines and a deposit scheme, for instance, may see litter fall sharply within a year.

In conclusion, providing convenient bins and enforcing penalties, together with education and deposit schemes, offers the most realistic way of reducing littering in public places.

essays.question: Many people say that human activity causes climate change. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Many people say that human activity causes climate change. I agree with this view, since the evidence links rising temperatures to emissions from industry and transport, and the speed of the change is hard to explain by natural cycles alone.

To begin with, scientific evidence links the recent rise in temperatures to human activity. Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, and temperatures have risen alongside emissions since the industrial era began. Natural cycles, such as volcanic activity and changes in the sun's output, operate over thousands of years, so they cannot account for such rapid warming. A greenhouse works in a similar way, which is why these gases are said to warm the planet.

Furthermore, the effects of human activity can be seen in everyday life. Cities full of cars and factories produce far more emissions than rural areas, and the loss of forests removes the trees that would absorb carbon dioxide. Rising sea levels, melting glaciers and more extreme weather have become more frequent in recent decades, which fits the pattern expected from added greenhouse gases. Admittedly, natural factors still influence the climate, but this is not the same as saying that people are not responsible. Recognising human causes is also useful, because it means that people can change the outcome by cutting emissions, protecting forests and investing in clean energy.

In conclusion, I agree that human activity causes climate change, because the evidence is strong and the speed of the warming points to human sources.

versions.text:
Many people say that human activity causes climate change. I agree with this view, since the evidence links rising temperatures to emissions from industry and transport, and the speed of the change is hard to explain by natural cycles alone.

To begin with, scientific evidence links the recent rise in temperatures to human activity. Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests release gases that trap heat in the atmosphere, and temperatures have risen alongside emissions since the industrial era began. Natural cycles, such as volcanic activity and changes in the sun's output, operate over thousands of years, so they cannot account for such rapid warming. A greenhouse works in a similar way, which is why these gases are said to warm the planet.

Furthermore, the effects of human activity can be seen in everyday life. Cities full of cars and factories produce far more emissions than rural areas, and the loss of forests removes the trees that would absorb carbon dioxide. Rising sea levels, melting glaciers and more extreme weather have become more frequent in recent decades, which fits the pattern expected from added greenhouse gases. Admittedly, natural factors still influence the climate, but this is not the same as saying that people are not responsible. Recognising human causes is also useful, because it means that people can change the outcome by cutting emissions, protecting forests and investing in clean energy. This practical point matters, since it turns a worrying fact into a reason for action. It also shows that the problem, although serious, is not beyond human control.

In conclusion, I agree that human activity causes climate change, because the evidence is strong and the speed of the warming points to human sources.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for energy conservation, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
As energy prices and emissions rise, people debate whether individuals should be responsible for saving energy or whether society and governments should take action. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, some argue that households should conserve energy because everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. People decide whether to leave lights and appliances on standby, how warm to keep their homes and how often to use the car. Switching to efficient bulbs, turning down the thermostat and unplugging unused devices can cut bills as well as emissions. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A household that lowers its heating by one degree and dries clothes on a line, for example, may notice a clear difference in its monthly bill, and the total saving across a whole city is considerable.

On the other hand, others believe that governments must act because individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. A tenant cannot insulate a landlord's building, and no consumer can choose clean electricity if the national grid still depends on coal. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as efficiency standards for appliances and buildings, and only they can invest in the renewable power and public transport that make low-energy living practical. A family in a poorly insulated rented flat, for instance, loses heat through the walls however careful it is.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that governments should take the lead by setting standards and funding improvements, while individuals make these policies effective through their daily habits.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on agricultural innovation? Use examples.

versions.text:
Farming has changed more in the last few decades than in the previous thousand years, thanks to new machines, seeds and software. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on agricultural innovation: higher output with fewer resources, and stronger rural communities.

First and foremost, agricultural innovation allows farmers to produce more with fewer resources. Drip irrigation, sensors and better seeds deliver water and fertiliser exactly where plants need them, so yields rise while waste falls. A farm that switches from flooding its fields to drip irrigation, for example, can grow the same crop with far less water, which matters in dry regions. As a result, the country can feed its growing population without clearing more forest or farmland, and it saves money on chemicals and fuel. Drones and satellite images also help farmers to spot disease early and treat only the affected area.

In addition, innovation strengthens rural economies. Higher output and lower costs raise farm incomes, and new technology creates skilled jobs in areas such as equipment maintenance, data analysis and food processing. Young people who might otherwise leave for cities can find attractive careers in the countryside, which keeps villages alive. A country that develops advanced farming methods can also sell its equipment and expertise to others. Although new technology may be expensive for small farmers, shared equipment and training schemes can spread the benefits widely.

To sum up, agricultural innovation brings clear benefits to a country, above all greater and more efficient food production and a more prosperous countryside. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: How far do you think renewable energy technology will become cheaper in the next 20 years? Support your answer with reasons.

versions.text:
Solar panels, wind turbines and batteries are becoming common, and I believe that renewable energy technology will become considerably cheaper over the next twenty years, although the pace may slow in some areas.

First and foremost, the main drivers of falling prices are likely to continue. As manufacturers build larger factories and produce more equipment, each panel or turbine costs less to make, and engineers keep finding ways to turn more sunlight and wind into electricity from the same machine. Competition between companies, especially in Asia, also pushes prices down. As a result, clean power that once needed subsidies can now compete with coal and gas in many places. A household that fits solar panels today, for example, pays much less than a neighbour did a decade ago, and this experience encourages other families to follow.

In addition, storage and grid technology are improving. Batteries have become cheaper as demand for electric vehicles has increased, which will lower the cost of keeping renewable power available at night. Better control systems will also reduce waste by matching supply with demand. However, costs will not fall in every area. Raw materials such as lithium and copper may become more expensive if mining cannot keep pace with demand, and higher interest rates make large projects costlier to finance. Connecting remote wind farms to cities also requires new power lines, which are expensive and slow to build. Prices may therefore fall more slowly than they did in the past.

In conclusion, renewable technology is likely to become cheaper to a large extent because of larger-scale production, competition and better storage, although material costs and grid investment could limit the speed of the decline.

essays.question: Discuss how community gardens benefit neighborhoods.

versions.text:
In many cities, small plots of land are used by residents to grow vegetables, herbs and flowers together. This essay will outline two key ways in which community gardens benefit neighbourhoods: by bringing people together and by providing fresh food and green space.

First and foremost, community gardens bring neighbours together. Residents grow vegetables on unused land, share skills and tools, and meet people from different backgrounds, which strengthens friendships and reduces loneliness. A vacant plot turned into a vegetable garden, for example, can become a place where neighbours meet instead of a spot where rubbish collects. Children learn where food comes from, and older residents pass on knowledge and enjoy the company. Working on a shared project builds trust, so neighbourhoods with such gardens often feel safer and friendlier, and people are more willing to help one another.

In addition, community gardens provide fresh food and improve the local environment. Households that grow their own produce save money on groceries and eat more vegetables, which supports healthy diets, especially in areas with few fresh food shops. The gardens also turn neglected land into green space that cools the air, shelters insects and birds and absorbs rainwater. Gardening is a gentle form of exercise and can reduce stress, which benefits mental wellbeing. Although a garden needs volunteers and some funding for tools and water, councils can help by lending land and offering advice, and the benefits to the neighbourhood far outweigh the small cost.

To sum up, community gardens benefit neighbourhoods by building community spirit and by providing fresh food and green space. For these reasons, they deserve continued public support.

essays.question: To what extent should product labelling include environmental impact information? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Shoppers are surrounded by information on packaging, from calories to country of origin, but very little of it tells them how a product affects the planet. I largely agree that product labelling should include environmental impact information, since it helps shoppers to choose better, although the system must be simple.

To begin with, environmental impact labels help shoppers to compare products. A simple rating for carbon emissions, water use or recyclability lets buyers choose better options and puts pressure on producers to improve. At present, buyers who want to reduce their impact often have to rely on advertising, which may be misleading. A shopper choosing between two similar bags of rice, for example, cannot tell which one involved more transport or more water unless the label says so. Clear information also helps to expose exaggerated green claims, which protects honest companies.

Furthermore, labels can change the market. When companies know that their ratings will be visible, they have a reason to reduce emissions and packaging, and those that perform well can use the label as a selling point. This is similar to the energy ratings on electrical appliances, which have encouraged manufacturers to make more efficient products. However, complicated or inconsistent labels may confuse shoppers and add costs, especially for small firms, and measuring the exact impact of every product is difficult. Governments should therefore require one clear, standard scheme, such as a colour scale, with independent checking and support for small businesses.

In conclusion, product labels should include environmental impact information to a large extent, because it supports informed choices and encourages better production, provided that the scheme is simple and reliable.

essays.question: Many people say that renewable energy investments create jobs. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Many governments now spend large sums on wind, solar and other clean power, and people say that this investment creates jobs. I largely agree with this view, since renewable projects need many workers at every stage, although some jobs in older industries may disappear.

To begin with, building and running renewable energy requires a wide range of workers. Factories make panels, turbine blades and batteries, construction crews build wind farms and solar parks, electricians install equipment on roofs and in substations, and technicians inspect and repair machines for decades afterwards. Many of these jobs are located in local communities rather than in distant cities, which spreads the benefit widely. A town that hosts a new wind farm, for example, may gain hundreds of jobs during construction and a smaller number of permanent posts for maintenance.

Furthermore, clean energy encourages new technology and related businesses. Companies that design software for smart grids, produce insulation or develop better batteries employ engineers and researchers, and a country that leads in these fields can sell its products abroad. Investment in this area also supports construction and transport firms that supply the projects. However, the picture is not entirely positive. Coal mines and power stations may close, and workers there cannot always move into new roles without help, because the skills required are different. Governments should therefore provide retraining and support for the regions affected, so that the gains are shared fairly.

In conclusion, I agree that renewable energy investments create jobs, especially in manufacturing, installation and maintenance, provided that workers in declining industries receive support.

Tuy nhiên, việc đề cập đến việc mất việc ở ngành cũ cần được tích hợp khéo léo hơn vào lập luận để giữ sự nhất quán.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on agriculture? Use examples.

versions.text:
Agriculture is often seen as an old-fashioned sector, yet it remains the foundation of every economy. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on agriculture: food security and a stable rural economy.

First and foremost, a strong farming sector protects a country's food security. A country that grows its own food depends less on imports and is less exposed to sudden price rises or supply problems on the world market. Reliable harvests also keep food affordable for ordinary families, which reduces hunger and protects public health. Countries that support their farmers during bad years, for example, can avoid shortages and keep prices stable. A nation that relies heavily on imported grain, in contrast, can find itself in difficulty when exporters restrict sales.

In addition, agriculture supports employment and rural stability. Farming, food processing, transport and equipment sales provide jobs and income for millions of people, particularly in areas with few other industries. This helps rural communities to remain viable, so that fewer people move to crowded cities in search of work, which in turn eases pressure on housing and services. Agricultural exports also earn foreign currency that can pay for imports of machinery and medicine. Because food is always in demand, the sector is relatively stable even when other industries face difficulties. Although farming depends on weather and is vulnerable to climate change, modern methods and insurance can reduce the risks.

To sum up, focusing on agriculture brings clear benefits to a country, above all food security and a stable rural economy. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Some people believe that nuclear energy is a safe and efficient power source. Others think it is dangerous. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether nuclear energy is a safe and efficient power source or a dangerous one. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that nuclear power is both safe and efficient. Statistically, it has caused far fewer deaths per unit of electricity than coal, which pollutes the air and harms the health of millions of people. It is also efficient, since a small amount of fuel produces a great deal of energy, and a plant can run day and night whatever the weather. Modern reactors include several layers of protection and are monitored closely by independent regulators. A country with strong safety rules, for example, can operate reactors for decades without a serious incident, while providing steady low-carbon electricity to homes and factories.

On the other hand, critics point out that the consequences of a nuclear accident can be severe and long-lasting. The disasters at Chernobyl and Fukushima forced thousands of people to leave their homes, and some areas remained unusable for years. Radioactive waste must also be stored for thousands of years, and there is a continuing fear that nuclear materials could be stolen or misused. These worries make many citizens uneasy about living near a plant. A rare error in a poorly regulated country, for instance, could affect a whole region.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that nuclear energy is reasonably safe and efficient where regulation is strong, although it must be accompanied by secure waste storage and open public information.

essays.question: Many people think that wildlife conservation has improved people’s lives. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Wildlife conservation is often seen as a luxury that benefits animals more than people. I agree that it has improved people's lives, since healthy ecosystems provide practical services and many communities earn a living from protected nature.

To begin with, wildlife conservation improves people's lives in practical ways. Healthy ecosystems pollinate crops, clean water and reduce floods, and these services would cost enormous sums to replace artificially. Bees that pollinate fruit trees, for example, help farmers to harvest more apples and almonds without any extra cost. Forests and wetlands protected for wildlife also store water and reduce the damage caused by storms. In addition, wild plants and animals provide the basis for new medicines, so losing a species may mean losing a future treatment.

Furthermore, conservation creates jobs and income. Nature tourism brings visitors to national parks and reserves, and local people work as guides, rangers, drivers and hotel staff. When communities share in these earnings, they have a reason to protect wildlife instead of hunting or clearing the land. Contact with nature also benefits mental health and offers children a chance to learn about the living world. Admittedly, conservation sometimes restricts land use and can cause conflict, as when elephants damage crops, but compensation schemes and community involvement can reduce these problems. Overall, the benefits to people, in food, water, income and wellbeing, are considerable and far-reaching.

In conclusion, I agree that wildlife conservation has improved people's lives, because it supports essential natural services and provides income, provided that local communities share fairly in the gains.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for wildlife conservation, or should society/government take action? Discuss.

versions.text:
Many species are now under threat, and people disagree about who should lead efforts to save them: individuals and communities, or the government. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal involvement argue that wildlife conservation succeeds only when ordinary people care about it. Local residents often know their area best, and volunteers who count birds, clean rivers or report injured animals provide help that no official body could afford. Donations to conservation charities also pay for projects that governments overlook. Public interest matters because it persuades politicians to act. A village that protects its own wetland and guides visitors around it, for example, can preserve the habitat while earning a modest income from tourism.

On the other hand, advocates of government action point out that conservation on a large scale needs money, laws and coordination that individuals cannot provide. Governments can create national parks, restrict building in sensitive areas and punish illegal hunting, and they alone can negotiate with other countries about species that cross borders, such as migrating birds. Charities and volunteers rely on limited and unpredictable funds, so a long-term plan needs public budgets. A rare species whose habitat is sold for development, for instance, cannot be saved by volunteers alone.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that governments should provide the legal and financial framework, while individuals and local groups supply the knowledge and enthusiasm that make conservation work.

essays.question: Do the advantages of nuclear power outweigh the environmental risks? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Concerns about climate change have revived interest in nuclear power, but it also raises environmental questions. This essay will discuss the advantages and disadvantages before explaining whether the advantages outweigh the risks.

On the positive side, nuclear power helps to reduce the environmental harm caused by fossil fuels. A reactor produces large amounts of electricity without releasing the greenhouse gases or the smoke that harms people's lungs, and it needs far less land than solar or wind farms to generate the same output. Replacing coal stations with nuclear plants can therefore cut carbon emissions and improve air quality at the same time. A city that closes a coal plant and opens a nuclear one, for example, may see a clear fall in air pollution within a few years.

On the negative side, nuclear power carries environmental risks of its own. Mining uranium damages land, and radioactive waste has to be stored safely for thousands of years. Plants also use large amounts of water for cooling, which can warm rivers and harm fish, and a serious accident would contaminate air, soil and water over a wide area. Nevertheless, these risks can be managed. Modern waste is small in volume and can be sealed deep underground, and strict regulation has made serious accidents extremely rare. In comparison, the damage from fossil fuels is certain, continuous and global, and it falls on every country.

In conclusion, the advantages of nuclear power outweigh its environmental risks, provided that governments invest in secure waste storage and independent safety checks.

essays.question: Some people believe that urban farming can solve food shortages. Others disagree. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether urban farming can solve food shortages. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters argue that urban farming brings fresh food closer to the people who eat it. Rooftop gardens, vertical farms and community plots use empty space in cities, cut transport distances and give residents access to fresh vegetables that would otherwise be expensive or hard to find. Local food costs less to deliver, loses less on the way and strengthens community ties, since neighbours work together and learn about growing. A block of flats that grows salad leaves on its roof, for example, can supply nearby households and restaurants throughout the year. In districts where fresh produce is scarce, this can improve diets and reduce hunger.

On the other hand, critics point out that urban farms cannot grow enough staple crops to end food shortages. Cities lack the land and water needed for wheat, rice and maize, which feed most of the world, and high rents and energy costs make indoor farms expensive. Most urban farms produce leafy vegetables and herbs, which are valuable but provide few calories. A large city that tried to feed itself from its own rooftops, for instance, would run out of space very quickly.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that urban farming is a useful supplement that improves access to fresh food, but it cannot replace rural agriculture or solve shortages on its own.
