essays.question: Some argue that strict environmental controls limit economic growth. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Some people claim that strict environmental controls limit economic growth. I agree only to a limited extent, since controls can raise costs in the short term, but they also protect the resources and health on which growth depends.

It is true that strict controls can raise costs for businesses and slow short-term growth. Factories must install cleaner equipment, and firms may respond by raising prices or cutting jobs, which matters most in poorer countries where growth is needed to lift people out of poverty. A small manufacturer that must buy expensive filters, for example, may find it hard to compete with a foreign rival that faces no such rule, and workers can lose their jobs as a result. These concerns should be taken seriously and should not be dismissed as mere excuses.

However, ignoring the environment is expensive in the long run. Floods, droughts and polluted air damage crops, homes and health, and the cost of cleaning up afterwards is usually far higher than the cost of preventing the damage. Environmental policy can also create growth, since renewable energy, insulation and recycling employ workers and encourage new technology. A country that leads in electric vehicles, for instance, can sell them abroad as well as improve its own air. Governments can also reduce the burden on business by introducing controls gradually and offering tax relief for clean equipment, so that companies have time to adapt.

In conclusion, strict environmental controls may slow growth briefly, but I do not accept that they limit it overall, since growth built on damage cannot last.

essays.question: Many feel that product packaging is wasteful and unnecessary. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Many products, from phones to cosmetics, arrive in boxes that are larger than the item and filled with plastic, paper and foam. I agree that much product packaging is wasteful and unnecessary, although some of it has a genuine purpose.

To begin with, a great deal of packaging exists mainly for marketing rather than protection. Attractive boxes, extra layers and oversized containers make products look more valuable, but they are discarded as soon as the item is opened. Online shopping adds more waste, as a small object may be sent in a large box filled with padding. A small bottle of perfume inside a box, a plastic case and a wrapping film, for example, uses far more material than the product needs. When millions of items are sold, this excess becomes a mountain of rubbish that councils must collect and dispose of.

Furthermore, this extra material has real costs for the environment. Making packaging consumes energy, water and raw materials, and much of it ends up in landfill or is burned, because mixed materials are hard to recycle. Larger boxes also take up more space in lorries, so more trips are needed to deliver the same goods. However, some packaging is necessary: fragile items such as glass or electronics need protection, and safe packaging prevents damage that would waste the product itself. The sensible answer is therefore not to abolish packaging but to design it better, using the smallest suitable size and materials that can be recycled. Governments could encourage this through standards and by making producers pay for the waste they create.

In conclusion, I agree that much product packaging is wasteful and unnecessary, but with better design and clear rules the problem can be reduced.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of pesticide use in agriculture.

versions.text:
Pesticides, which are chemicals used to kill insects, weeds and fungi, are applied to crops in almost every farming region. This essay will discuss the main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, pesticides protect crops from insects, weeds and disease. Without them farmers could lose a large share of their harvest, which would raise food prices and leave more people hungry. They also allow fruit and vegetables to look attractive and to last longer in shops, so less food is thrown away. A grower whose orchard is hit by a destructive insect, for example, may lose most of the fruit within weeks unless the pest is controlled. For many families, cheaper and more reliable food is a real benefit.

On the negative side, however, pesticides can harm people, wildlife and water. Residues may stay on food, chemicals wash into rivers and kill useful insects such as bees, and pests gradually become resistant, which forces farmers to use stronger products. Farm workers who handle these chemicals without protection may also suffer from illness. Nevertheless, the harm can be reduced. Integrated pest management, which combines natural predators, crop rotation and small amounts of spraying only when needed, protects harvests while using far fewer chemicals. Strict rules on which products are allowed and on safe use would also help.

In conclusion, pesticides play an important role in feeding the world, but their effects on health and the environment are serious. On balance, I believe that they should be used sparingly and under strict control, alongside safer methods.

essays.question: Some believe that banning single-use plastics is effective. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Many countries have banned items such as plastic bags, straws and cutlery, and some people believe that these bans are an effective way of dealing with plastic pollution. I largely agree, although a ban works best when it is part of a wider approach.

To begin with, bans change behaviour quickly and reduce litter. When a product is no longer available, people have to use alternatives, and the effect is immediate rather than gradual. Places that have charged for or banned plastic bags generally report that their use falls sharply and that fewer bags are found on beaches and in rivers. A shop that can no longer give out plastic cutlery, for example, will switch to wooden or reusable alternatives, and customers soon accept the change. Bans also send a clear signal that society regards wasteful products as unacceptable, which encourages businesses to invest in better materials.

However, bans are not enough on their own. Some substitutes, such as paper or thick cotton bags, need more energy to produce, so the environmental benefit depends on people reusing them many times. Enforcement can also be weak, particularly among small sellers and markets, and plastic from other sources, such as packaging and fishing nets, continues to pollute. Bans should therefore be combined with deposit schemes, better recycling and public education, and with support for businesses that must change. Without these measures, banned items may simply be replaced by others that cause similar harm.

In conclusion, banning single-use plastics is effective to a large extent in cutting litter quickly, but it needs the support of other measures to deal with the whole problem.

essays.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of biofuels.

versions.text:
Biofuels, which are made from crops, waste and other plant material, are increasingly mixed with petrol and diesel. This essay will discuss their main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, biofuels can reduce the carbon emissions of transport. Plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, so in theory the fuel releases about the same amount that it removed from the air, which makes it cleaner over its life than oil. It can also be used in existing engines and fuel stations with little change, so countries do not have to replace all their vehicles at once. In addition, growing fuel crops supports farmers and reduces dependence on imported oil. A country that blends plant-based fuel into its petrol, for example, can cut emissions from millions of cars quickly, long before electric vehicles become common.

On the negative side, biofuels raise serious concerns about land and food. Fuel crops need farmland, so they may compete with food production and push up prices, which hurts poorer families most. If forests are cleared to plant them, the carbon released can cancel out the benefits. Growing, fertilising and processing crops also consumes energy and water. Biofuels made from waste, such as used cooking oil, avoid many of these problems, but supplies are limited.

In conclusion, biofuels offer a useful way to cut transport emissions, but their effect on land and food prices is a real drawback. On balance, I believe that they should be developed mainly from waste materials, while other options such as electric vehicles receive greater support.

versions.text:
Biofuels, which are made from crops, waste and other plant material, are increasingly mixed with petrol and diesel. This essay will discuss their main advantages and disadvantages before explaining my own view.

On the positive side, biofuels can reduce the carbon emissions of transport. Plants absorb carbon dioxide as they grow, so in theory the fuel releases about the same amount that it removed from the air, which makes it cleaner over its life than oil. It can also be used in existing engines and fuel stations with little change, so countries do not have to replace all their vehicles at once. In addition, growing fuel crops supports farmers and reduces dependence on imported oil. A country that blends plant-based fuel into its petrol, for example, can cut emissions from millions of cars quickly, long before electric vehicles become common.

On the negative side, biofuels raise serious concerns about land and food. Fuel crops need farmland, so they may compete with food production and push up prices, which hurts poorer families most. If forests are cleared to plant them, the carbon released can cancel out the benefits. Growing, fertilising and processing crops also consumes energy and water. Biofuels made from waste, such as used cooking oil, avoid many of these problems, but supplies are limited. Research into fuels from algae and farm residues may widen the supply in future.

In conclusion, biofuels offer a useful way to cut transport emissions, but their effect on land and food prices is a real drawback. On balance, I believe that they should be developed mainly from waste materials, while other options such as electric vehicles receive greater support.

essays.question: Some argue that shorter product life cycles harm the environment. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Phones, clothes and appliances are replaced more quickly than ever, and some people argue that shorter product life cycles harm the environment. I largely agree, since faster replacement increases resource use and waste, although newer products can sometimes be more efficient.

To begin with, making a new product uses large amounts of energy, water and raw materials. Most of a phone's environmental impact, for example, comes from mining and manufacturing rather than from daily use, so replacing it after two years instead of five increases that impact. When products are designed to be replaced quickly, with sealed batteries or fashionable styles that go out of date, more items are produced and discarded. Electronic waste, which contains harmful substances, is increasing faster than almost any other type of rubbish, and much of it is not recycled.

Furthermore, shorter life cycles encourage a throwaway culture. When goods are cheap and quickly outdated, people see little point in repairing them, so working items are discarded and landfill sites fill up. Admittedly, new models can be more energy efficient, and fast-moving markets may drive innovation and create jobs. For some products, such as refrigerators, replacing a very old model can save energy. However, these gains are usually smaller than the harm caused by constantly manufacturing new goods. Governments could encourage durable design by requiring repairable products, longer warranties and clear information about expected lifespan, so that buyers can choose items that last.

In conclusion, shorter product life cycles harm the environment to a large extent, because they raise resource use and waste, although efficiency gains in some products should be recognised.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for reporting environmental violations, or should society/government act proactively? Discuss.

versions.text:
When factories dump waste or forests are cut down illegally, it is not always clear who should act: citizens who report what they see, or authorities that look for violations themselves. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of public reporting argue that ordinary people are often the first to notice environmental damage. Residents see the smoke from a chimney, the discoloured river or the lorry unloading rubbish at night, and no inspector can be everywhere at once. Reports from the public therefore extend the reach of the authorities at low cost. A community that can report problems easily is also more likely to feel responsible for its surroundings. A fisherman who notices a poisoned stream and phones a hotline, for example, may stop pollution before it spreads to the whole river.

On the other hand, advocates of proactive government action point out that relying on individuals puts the burden on the wrong people. Citizens may not recognise a violation, may fear punishment from a local employer or may simply not bother, so serious offences can go undetected for years. Authorities can carry out regular inspections, use satellite monitoring and impose penalties that deter companies in the first place. An employee who fears losing a job, for instance, is unlikely to report their own factory.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that governments should act proactively and enforce the rules, while making reporting easy and safe so that the public can help.

Các luận điểm cho cả hai bên đều được phát triển hợp lý với các ví dụ cụ thể, tuy nhiên phần kết luận có thể mở rộng sâu hơn một chút về sự kết hợp giữa hai bên.

essays.question: Some people say that recycling should be mandatory. Do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Many households still throw recyclable materials into the general bin, and some people say that recycling should be made mandatory. I agree with this view, since voluntary schemes have not achieved high participation, although compulsion must be accompanied by good services.

To begin with, mandatory recycling creates much higher participation. When recycling is optional, many people ignore it because it takes effort and the benefit seems small, so valuable materials end up in landfill. A clear legal requirement, backed by modest fines or by collection rules that refuse mixed rubbish, turns recycling into a normal habit, in the same way that seat belts became normal once they were compulsory. Higher volumes also supply recycling plants with the material they need to operate profitably, which keeps costs down. A district that requires sorting at the kerb, for example, may recycle far more than one that merely asks residents to take part.

Furthermore, a rule shows that society regards waste as a shared responsibility. Without it, careful households bear the effort while others do nothing, which is unfair. However, compulsion works only if people are given the means to comply. Authorities must provide convenient collection, clear instructions and bins of the right size, and they should begin with warnings and education rather than immediate penalties. Rules that are too strict or too complicated may cause resentment and poor sorting, so contaminated loads can end up wasted anyway. Introduced fairly and explained well, mandatory recycling is a sensible step that most communities will accept after a short time.

In conclusion, I agree that recycling should be mandatory, because voluntary action has not been enough, provided that the rules are supported by easy services and sensible enforcement.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on climate adaptation or climate mitigation? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether governments should spend more on adapting to climate change or on trying to reduce it. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of adaptation argue that it protects people from harm that is already happening. Sea walls, flood defences, drought-resistant crops and early warning systems save lives and homes within a few years, whereas cuts in emissions take decades to change the climate. Adaptation also helps countries that produce little pollution but suffer its effects, such as small island nations. A coastal town that builds a flood barrier, for example, protects its residents from the next storm, whatever the world does about emissions, and the investment begins to pay back as soon as the barrier is finished.

On the other hand, advocates of mitigation point out that adaptation alone only treats the symptoms. Cutting emissions at their source, through renewable energy, efficient buildings and cleaner transport, reduces the scale of the problem, whereas defences become more expensive and less effective as temperatures rise. Prevention is also far cheaper than dealing with the consequences later, and clean technology can create growth and jobs. A country that relies only on higher sea walls, for instance, must keep rebuilding them as the sea continues to rise.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that mitigation should receive the larger share, since it tackles the cause, although vulnerable communities must still be protected through adaptation.

feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú, sử dụng chính xác các thuật ngữ chuyên ngành về môi trường như 'climate adaptation', 'climate mitigation', 'drought-resistant crops', 'emissions'. Các cụm từ kết hợp (collocations) tự nhiên và phù hợp với văn phong học thuật.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc ngữ pháp đa dạng bao gồm câu ghép, câu phức với các mệnh đề quan hệ và trạng ngữ chỉ nhượng bộ. Các lỗi ngữ pháp hầu như không xuất hiện, độ chính xác cao.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether governments should spend more on adapting to climate change or on trying to reduce it. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of adaptation argue that it protects people from harm that is already happening. Sea walls, flood defences, drought-resistant crops and early warning systems save lives and homes within a few years, whereas cuts in emissions take decades to change the climate. Adaptation also helps countries that produce little pollution but suffer its effects, such as small island nations. A coastal town that builds a flood barrier, for example, protects its residents from the next storm, whatever the world does about emissions, and the investment begins to pay back as soon as the barrier is finished.

On the other hand, advocates of mitigation point out that adaptation alone only treats the symptoms. Cutting emissions at their source, through renewable energy, efficient buildings and cleaner transport, reduces the scale of the problem, whereas defences become more expensive and less effective as temperatures rise. Prevention is also far cheaper than dealing with the consequences later, and clean technology can create growth and jobs. A country that relies only on higher sea walls, for instance, must keep rebuilding them as the sea continues to rise. Moreover, long-term projects such as grid upgrades take many years, so delay would make the task harder and more costly.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that mitigation should receive the larger share, since it tackles the cause, although vulnerable communities must still be protected through adaptation.

essays.question: What are the benefits for a country that focuses on clean water access? Use examples.

versions.text:
Hundreds of millions of people still lack a safe and reliable water supply. This essay will outline two principal benefits for a country that focuses on clean water access: better health and wider opportunities for education and work.

First and foremost, clean water protects health. Safe drinking water prevents diseases such as diarrhoea and cholera, which kill many young children, and proper sanitation stops infections from spreading. As a result, fewer people become ill, hospitals are less crowded and families spend less on medicine. A village that gains a safe tap, for example, sees fewer children miss school because of stomach illness, and healthier adults are able to work more regularly. In the long term, a healthy population is also cheaper for the country to support.

In addition, clean water frees time for education and work. Where there is no tap nearby, women and girls often spend several hours every day carrying water, which stops them from attending school or earning money. Piped water removes this burden, so more girls can complete their education and more adults can take paid jobs. Reliable water also supports farming, food processing and manufacturing, which raises productivity and attracts investment. Healthier, better-educated people make the economy stronger, and the benefits continue across generations. Although building pipes and treatment plants requires large investment, studies in many countries suggest that the returns in health and productivity are far greater than the cost.

To sum up, clean water access brings clear benefits to a country, above all better health and wider opportunities. For these reasons, it deserves sustained public support.

essays.question: Many feel that fast fashion harms the environment. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
Cheap clothes that change with every season are available in almost every high street, and many people feel that fast fashion harms the environment. I agree with this view, since the industry encourages overconsumption and creates large amounts of waste and pollution.

To begin with, fast fashion encourages people to buy more clothes than they need. Cheap, quickly changing styles lead to overproduction, high water and energy use, synthetic fibres that release microplastics, and large amounts of discarded clothing. A cheap dress that is worn twice and then thrown away, for example, wastes the water and energy used to make it. Producing cotton uses a great deal of water, and dyeing fabrics can pollute rivers if factories are poorly regulated. Because clothes are sold at very low prices, shoppers treat them as disposable, and much of what is thrown away ends up in landfill or is burned.

Furthermore, the damage is increased by the speed and scale of the industry. Garments are made far from where they are sold and transported across the world, which adds emissions, and many are poorly made so that they fall apart after a few washes. Admittedly, the fashion industry provides jobs, and affordable clothes are valuable for families on low incomes. However, these benefits do not require such rapid turnover. Consumers can buy fewer, better-made items, choose second-hand clothes and repair what they own, while governments can require companies to take responsibility for waste and for pollution in their supply chains.

In conclusion, I agree that fast fashion harms the environment, because it drives overconsumption and waste, although changes in shopping habits and stronger regulation could reduce the damage.

essays.question: Many people say that public beaches should be preserved from development. Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons and examples.

versions.text:
Beaches are among the most popular public places, but many coastlines are now being lined with hotels, apartments and private clubs. I agree that public beaches should be preserved from development, since they are a shared resource that protects the coast and should stay open to everyone.

To begin with, public beaches should stay open to everyone. Building along the shore privatises access, so that ordinary families are shut out of places that were once free to enjoy. Beaches offer cheap recreation and exercise for people of all incomes, and restricting access creates a divide between those who can afford a sea view and those who cannot. A resort that blocks the path to the water with fences and security guards, for example, turns a public place into a private one. Once access is lost, it is rarely regained.

Furthermore, building on or near the shore damages the natural features that protect people and wildlife. Sand dunes act as barriers against storms and floods, and construction can remove them, speed up erosion and increase the risk to nearby homes. Lights, noise and crowds also disturb nesting birds and turtles. Well-managed beaches keep attracting visitors and income without permanent damage. Admittedly, development brings jobs and tourist spending, and some facilities such as toilets and cafes are useful. However, a limited amount of simple, low-impact building set back from the shore can provide most of these benefits, while keeping the beach itself open and natural.

In conclusion, I agree that public beaches should be preserved from development, because they belong to everyone and protect the coast, although small, carefully planned facilities can be allowed.

essays.question: Some believe that ocean conservation should be a global priority. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

versions.text:
Plastic waste, overfishing and rising temperatures are damaging the world's seas, and some people believe that ocean conservation should be a global priority. I largely agree, since the ocean is shared by all countries and supports human life, although other urgent problems must not be neglected.

To begin with, the ocean is a shared resource that no single country can protect alone. Fish stocks, currents and pollution cross borders, so action by one nation can be undone by another. Fishing fleets that empty a region's waters, for example, leave coastal communities in other countries with fewer fish. Only international agreements, shared monitoring and common rules can prevent such harm. A global priority also encourages richer countries to help poorer ones to protect their coastlines.

Furthermore, the sea provides food for billions of people and helps to regulate the climate and produce oxygen. If marine ecosystems collapse, millions of people who depend on fishing and coastal tourism would lose their income and their main source of protein. Healthy oceans also absorb large amounts of carbon dioxide, which slows climate change. However, ocean conservation cannot be the only priority. Governments also face poverty, health care and education, and enforcement across huge areas of open water is difficult. Realistic goals, such as protected zones, catch limits and stronger rules on plastic, together with funding for poorer countries, would make conservation both effective and fair.

In conclusion, ocean conservation should be a global priority to a large extent, because the sea is shared and essential for human life, provided that it is balanced with other urgent needs.

essays.question: To what extent should governments limit single-use packaging? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Takeaway boxes, wrappers and shopping bags are used for minutes but remain in the environment for years. I largely agree that governments should limit single-use packaging, since voluntary action by companies has not been enough, although the rules must be realistic.

To begin with, only governments can create rules that apply to everyone. If one supermarket reduces packaging while its rivals do not, it may lose customers or face higher costs, so businesses have little reason to act alone. Laws, taxes and fines create a level playing field in which responsible firms are not undercut by careless ones. Limits on unnecessary wrapping and charges for disposable items also change habits at a scale that appeals to individuals cannot reach. A requirement that restaurants use reusable containers for customers who eat in, for example, would remove millions of items from the waste stream and cost very little to administer.

Furthermore, limiting packaging protects the environment and saves public money. Councils spend large sums collecting and processing rubbish, and litter damages rivers, beaches and wildlife. Producers can be required to pay for the waste they create, which encourages them to design simpler, recyclable packaging. However, limits should not go so far that food becomes unsafe or spoils faster, because that would increase food waste. Exceptions for medical products and perishable foods, and transition periods for small firms, would make the rules fair and practical. Governments should also review the results regularly, so that rules can be adjusted if they cause unexpected problems.

In conclusion, governments should limit single-use packaging to a large extent, because voluntary action is not enough and the damage is costly, provided that the rules protect safety and give businesses time to adapt.

essays.question: Many feel that product warranties should be longer to reduce waste. Do you agree? Explain your view.

versions.text:
A product that breaks just after its guarantee ends is likely to be thrown away, and many people feel that warranties should be longer in order to reduce waste. I agree with this view, since longer warranties encourage better products and make repair more common.

To begin with, longer warranties give manufacturers a reason to build durable goods. If a company must repair or replace its products for five years instead of one, it will use stronger parts and better testing, because failures become costly. Products that last longer mean fewer items are made and discarded, which saves energy, water and raw materials. A washing machine with a ten-year guarantee, for example, is likely to be built to last, and its owner does not need to buy a replacement after two years. Over time, durable design would reduce the pile of broken goods that councils must handle.

Furthermore, longer warranties make repair the normal choice. When a fault is covered, customers return the product for repair instead of throwing it away, and companies develop repair services and supply spare parts. Consumers also benefit, since they spend less on replacements. Admittedly, longer guarantees may raise the initial price, and some firms might try to avoid claims. However, honest firms can recover the cost through lower replacement rates and stronger customer loyalty, and governments can set minimum standards and penalise those who refuse legitimate repairs. Clear rules would protect both buyers and sellers, and would make long-lasting products a selling point instead of a rarity.

In conclusion, I agree that warranties should be longer, because this encourages durable design and repair, which reduces waste, provided that clear rules prevent firms from avoiding their responsibilities.

essays.question: What are the causes of food waste in developed countries? What solutions can be proposed?

versions.text:
Wealthy countries throw away large quantities of edible food every day, which wastes money and resources. This essay will analyse the principal causes and propose realistic solutions.

Overbuying and strict rules about appearance and dates are major causes of food waste. Shoppers often buy more than they need, attracted by bulk offers and large packs, and food then spoils in the fridge before it can be eaten. Many people also misunderstand date labels and discard products that are still safe. In addition, supermarkets and producers reject fruit and vegetables that are the wrong size or shape, even though they taste the same, and restaurants serve portions that are larger than customers can finish. A bag of misshapen carrots that never reaches the shelf, for example, is wasted before anyone has a chance to eat it.

To address this issue, governments should require clearer labels and encourage retailers to sell imperfect produce at lower prices. Laws or incentives can make supermarkets pass unsold but edible food to charities and food banks, as some countries already do, so that surplus feeds people instead of landfill. Education campaigns in schools and on social media can teach households to plan meals, store food properly and use leftovers. Councils can also provide food-waste collection for composting or energy production. These measures are inexpensive compared with the money and resources lost when food is thrown away, and they help families to cut their grocery bills.

In conclusion, food waste in developed countries stems mainly from overbuying and from strict appearance and date standards, but clearer labels, redistribution of surplus and education offer a realistic way forward.

essays.question: Some argue that stricter animal protection laws benefit society. To what extent do you agree?

versions.text:
Some countries have strict laws against cruelty to animals while others have almost none, and some argue that stricter animal protection laws benefit society as well as animals. I largely agree, although the benefits depend on laws being enforced fairly.

To begin with, stricter animal protection laws benefit society as well as animals. Respect for animals teaches children compassion, and researchers have found links between cruelty to animals and violence towards people, so laws that take cruelty seriously may help to prevent wider harm. Better conditions on farms can also reduce the risk of disease spreading among animals and into the human population, and they improve food safety. A farm that keeps animals in clean, spacious housing, for example, usually needs fewer antibiotics, which helps to slow the spread of drug-resistant infections.

Furthermore, strong laws support the economy in certain areas. Countries with good records on animal welfare attract responsible tourists and consumers who are willing to pay more for ethical products, and businesses that meet high standards gain a reputation for quality. Clear rules also create a level playing field, so that careful producers are not undercut by careless ones. However, stricter laws can raise costs for farmers and small businesses, and enforcement requires trained inspectors, which governments must fund. Support, advice and transition periods can reduce the burden on producers. If these conditions are met, the gains for society, in health, values and trade, clearly outweigh the costs.

In conclusion, stricter animal protection laws benefit society to a large extent, since they promote compassion, safer food and fair competition, provided that they are enforced fairly and supported by help for producers.

essays.question: Many people think that DIY culture encourages sustainability. Do you agree? Explain with examples.

versions.text:
Repairing a bicycle, making shelves from old planks or sewing a torn jacket was once ordinary, and today do-it-yourself, or DIY, activities are returning. I largely agree that DIY culture encourages sustainability, although its effect is limited without wider change.

To begin with, do-it-yourself culture encourages people to repair and reuse instead of throwing away. Fixing a broken item, making furniture from old materials or sharing tools extends the life of products, saves money and teaches useful skills. A neighbourhood repair cafe, for instance, lets residents mend toasters and bicycles together instead of buying replacements. Less waste is produced and fewer new goods have to be made, which saves energy and raw materials. People who have repaired something themselves also tend to value it more and are less likely to discard it casually.

Furthermore, DIY activities change attitudes. When people see how things are built and how they fail, they start to question disposable products and demand items that can be repaired. Online videos, workshops and tool libraries make it easier than ever to learn. However, the effect of this culture is limited. Not everyone has the skills, tools or time to repair things, some repairs are unsafe, and the largest environmental impacts come from industry and transport rather than from households. DIY should therefore complement, not replace, wider changes such as durable design, the right to repair and cleaner production.

In conclusion, DIY culture encourages sustainability to a large extent by reducing waste and changing attitudes, but its effect is limited unless governments and companies also act.

essays.question: How can governments encourage homeowners to improve insulation? Suggest practical measures.

versions.text:
Heating and cooling homes uses a large share of a country's energy, and a poorly insulated house wastes much of it. This essay will suggest practical measures that governments could take, focusing on reducing the cost of insulation and on setting rules and giving advice.

To begin with, governments can make home insulation cheaper and easier. Grants, low-interest loans and tax rebates remove the high upfront cost, which is the main reason many families delay improvements, and local schemes can offer to install insulation at a reduced price. A family that insulates its loft and walls, for example, may notice a clear fall in its heating bills within a single winter. Because the savings continue every year, the payments can often be recovered over time. Targeted help for low-income households is especially valuable, since they spend a larger share of their income on energy.

In addition, authorities should use rules and information to encourage action. Minimum standards for new buildings and rented homes ensure that landlords cannot ignore the problem, because tenants often cannot make improvements themselves. Free energy checks show owners what to fix first, and a clear rating on every property helps buyers and renters to compare homes. Public campaigns can explain how much money and energy can be saved, and training for local builders makes sure that work is done properly. Together, these measures help households to save money while national emissions fall, and the cost to the government is modest compared with building new power stations.

In conclusion, cutting the cost of insulation and combining standards with advice offer the most realistic way of encouraging homeowners to improve insulation.

essays.question: Should individuals be responsible for reducing e-waste, or should society/government enforce recycling? Discuss.

versions.text:
Discarded phones, computers and televisions are creating a fast-growing waste problem, and opinions differ on whether people should be responsible for reducing it or whether the state should enforce recycling. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Consumers decide how often to replace a device, whether to repair it and where to dispose of it, and a phone left in a drawer or thrown into household rubbish wastes valuable materials. Buyers who choose durable products also push manufacturers to improve their designs. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A student who repairs a cracked screen instead of buying a new phone, for example, keeps a device in use for several more years, and millions of similar choices would greatly reduce the pile of electronic waste.

On the other hand, advocates of enforcement point out that individuals alone cannot solve problems that are largely structural. Most people do not know where to take an old device, and many products are deliberately designed to be difficult to repair. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as requiring manufacturers to take back what they sell, and only they can build collection systems and licensed recycling plants. A household with no drop-off point nearby, for instance, will probably keep or discard the device rather than travel far.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that governments should enforce recycling and make producers responsible, since this removes the burden from consumers, while individuals support it by repairing and returning their devices.

essays.question: To what extent should food origin be labelled on products? Give reasons for your answer.

versions.text:
Shoppers today buy food that has often travelled thousands of kilometres, and many of them have no idea where it was grown. I largely agree that food origin should be labelled on products, since labels help shoppers to make informed choices, although the rules should not be too costly.

To begin with, labels showing where food comes from help shoppers to make informed choices. Buyers can support local farmers, avoid products linked to poor safety records or very long transport, and decide whether they are willing to pay more for particular regions. If a problem such as contamination occurs, a clear origin also makes it easier to trace the source and withdraw the product quickly. A shopper who reads that apples were grown in a nearby region, for example, may choose them over apples flown from another continent, which reduces transport emissions.

Furthermore, labelling gives producers a reason to meet higher standards. When customers can see the origin, farmers and companies are more careful about quality and honesty, because their reputation is visible. It also protects consumers from misleading claims, such as a product described as local when only the packaging was done nearby. However, there are costs. Small producers may find complicated labelling expensive, and origin does not always indicate quality, since good and bad products exist in every country. Rules should therefore be simple and consistent, and phased in with support for small businesses.

In conclusion, food origin should be labelled to a large extent, because it improves choice and accountability, provided that the rules are clear and affordable.

grade.summary: Bài viết hoàn thành tốt yêu cầu đề bài với lập trường rõ ràng, cấu trúc mạch lạc và vốn từ vựng, ngữ pháp tốt. Tuy nhiên, việc tinh chỉnh một số cụm từ và làm sâu sắc thêm lập luận sẽ giúp bài viết đạt điểm cao hơn.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on organic farming or on other priorities? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be spent on organic farming or on other priorities such as health and education. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of organic farming argue that it reduces chemical use and protects soil and wildlife. Organic farmers avoid synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, which keeps soil healthy, protects rivers from chemical runoff and supports insects, birds and other wildlife. Many consumers also prefer organic food and are willing to pay more for it, so public support can help farmers to enter a growing market. A farm that rotates crops and uses natural compost, for example, may improve its soil year after year while producing food with fewer chemical residues.

On the other hand, critics point out that governments have limited funds and many equally urgent responsibilities. Hospitals, schools, housing and welfare all need money now, and organic farming has drawbacks. Yields are usually lower, so more land is needed to produce the same amount of food, and organic products are often more expensive, which makes them hard to afford for poorer families. Spending large sums on one method of farming may therefore bring little benefit compared with spending on public services. A town with overcrowded classrooms, for instance, has more pressing needs than a grant for organic growers.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that other priorities should receive most of the budget, with modest and targeted support for sustainable farming where the environmental benefits are clear.

essays.question: Is it better to focus government spending on climate change or on other priorities? Discuss and give your opinion.

versions.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether public money should be directed mainly at climate change or at other priorities such as health and education. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of other priorities argue that governments have limited funds and many equally urgent responsibilities. Hospitals, schools, housing and welfare all need money now, and a patient waiting for treatment or a child in an overcrowded classroom cannot wait for the long-term benefits of climate policy. In poorer countries especially, spending heavily on emissions cuts may seem a luxury when basic needs are unmet. A town with no emergency hospital, for example, has more pressing needs than a new solar farm.

On the other hand, advocates of climate spending point out that ignoring the environment is expensive in the long run. Floods, heatwaves and droughts destroy homes and farmland, and the cost of repairing the damage later is usually far higher than the cost of preventing it. Climate spending can also create growth and jobs in renewable energy, insulation and public transport, and it reduces illness caused by air pollution, so it supports health as well as the environment. A government that builds flood defences today, for instance, saves far more than it spends when a storm arrives.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that climate action deserves a substantial share of spending, because its costs rise the longer it is delayed, while essential services must still be protected.

Delay is therefore a costly choice, because every year without action locks in more emissions that later governments must pay to remove.

grade.summary: Bài viết của bạn rất có cấu trúc, diễn đạt tự nhiên và đáp ứng tốt yêu cầu của đề bài thảo luận hai chiều. Các ý tưởng được triển khai mạch lạc với văn phong học thuật phù hợp.
weaknesses: Quan điểm cá nhân ở phần kết luận hơi an toàn và có phần lập lờ khi vừa muốn chi cho khí hậu vừa muốn bảo vệ dịch vụ thiết yếu.
Một số từ vựng có tính lặp lại (spending, money).

feedback.taskResponse: Bài viết đã thảo luận tốt cả hai quan điểm và đưa ra quan điểm cá nhân rõ ràng ở phần mở đầu và kết luận. Các luận điểm được phát triển logic và có ví dụ minh họa cụ thể.
feedback.coherenceCohesion: Bố cục bài viết mạch lạc với các đoạn văn rõ ràng, sử dụng các từ nối chuyển ý tự nhiên và hiệu quả. Các ý tưởng được sắp xếp theo trình tự logic từ các mặt đối lập đến quan điểm cá nhân.
feedback.lexicalResource: Vốn từ vựng phong phú, sử dụng nhiều cụm từ chính xác liên quan đến chủ đề (emissions cuts, long-term benefits, flood defences). Tuy nhiên, có thể bổ sung thêm một số từ vựng nâng cao hơn để đạt band cao hơn.
feedback.grammar: Cấu trúc ngữ pháp đa dạng, từ câu đơn đến câu phức được sử dụng chính xác. Độ trôi chảy ngữ pháp rất tốt, hầu như không có lỗi sai cơ bản nào.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: chi tiêu chính phủ cho biến đổi khí hậu hay ưu tiên khác

plan.think: Khung hai quan điểm; đối ứng với đề 31 (giáo dục vs ưu tiên khác) nên dùng lại cấu trúc 'limited funds / equally urgent'.
Ngân sách có hạn: bệnh viện, trường học, nhà ở. Ví dụ thị trấn không có bệnh viện cấp cứu cần hơn trang trại điện mặt trời.
Bỏ qua môi trường đắt về lâu dài; việc làm; giảm bệnh do ô nhiễm. Ví dụ đê chống lũ.
Khí hậu xứng đáng một phần đáng kể vì chi phí tăng khi trì hoãn, nhưng dịch vụ thiết yếu vẫn phải được bảo vệ.
